extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy / political theory
extracted.subtask_description: A passage from Plato's Republic (Book II) that poses challenges about the nature and value of justice, proposes probing justice first at the level of a constructed State and then in the individual, and sets out illustrative thought‑experiments (e.g., Gyges' ring) and social origins (division of labour, luxury) to test those claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold classification of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: How would you arrange goods—are there not some which we welcome for their own sakes ... Is there not also a second class of goods, such as knowledge, sight, health, which are desirable not only in themselves, but also for their results? And would you not recognize a third class, such as gymnastic, and the care of the sick, and the physician’s art; also the various ways of money‑making—these do us good but we regard them as disagreeable; and no one would choose them for their own sakes, but only for the sake of some reward or result which flows from them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the conceptual criterion for evaluating whether something (here: justice) is to be valued for itself, for its consequences, or only as instrumentally useful; examples in each class are given (harmless pleasures; knowledge, sight, health; unpleasant but useful tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of justice as a compromise / lesser evil
rubrics_metrics.description: They say that to do injustice is, by nature, good; to suffer injustice, evil; but that the evil is greater than the good. And so when men have both done and suffered injustice and have had experience of both, not being able to avoid the one and obtain the other, they think that they had better agree among themselves to have neither; hence there arise laws and mutual covenants; and that which is ordained by law is termed by them lawful and just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the common view that justice arises as a social contract/compromise to avoid the greater evil; frames a criterion for judging popular moral accounts (justice as tolerated, not as a genuine good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as voluntary vs. involuntary (Gyges' ring argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you could imagine any one obtaining this power of becoming invisible, and never doing any wrong or touching what was another’s, he would be thought ... to be a most wretched idiot ... no man would keep his hands off what was not his own when he could safely take what he liked ... Then the actions of the just would be as the actions of the unjust; they would both come at last to the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the thought‑experiment of Gyges' ring to test whether justice is chosen for its own sake or only from fear of detection/punishment; methodological test for claims about the motives for justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of the 'perfectly unjust' life
rubrics_metrics.description: In the perfectly unjust man we must assume the most perfect injustice; there is to be no deduction, but we must allow him, while doing the most unjust acts, to have acquired the greatest reputation for justice ... he must be one who can speak with effect, if any of his deeds come to light, and who can force his way where force is required by his courage and strength, and command of money and friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets criteria for the hypothetical ideal‑type of an entirely unjust person (skill, ability to conceal wrongdoing, reputation for justice, resources, rhetorical and coercive competence) so that the comparison with the just life is not biased by incompetence or detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of the 'perfectly just' life
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him be the best of men, and let him be thought the worst; then he will have been put to the proof ... let him be clothed in justice only, and have no other covering ... wishing, as Aeschylus says, to be and not to seem good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the ideal just person as one who is just for its own sake (not for reputation or reward) and who remains just even when misjudged or punished — a methodological requirement for testing the intrinsic value of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate and compare extreme lives as a judgement method
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, if we are to form a real judgment of the life of the just and unjust, we must isolate them; ... Let the unjust man be entirely unjust, and the just man entirely just; nothing is to be taken away from either of them, and both are to be perfectly furnished for the work of their respective lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes an evaluative method: to fairly judge whether justice is better, compare fully realized extremes (no partialities) so that external confounders (reputation, incompetence) are removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical/eulogistic case for injustice (advantages claimed for the unjust)
rubrics_metrics.description: They will tell you that the just man who is thought unjust will be scourged, racked, bound—will have his eyes burnt out ... The unjust is pursuing a reality; he does not live with a view to appearances—he wants to be really unjust and not to seem only: ... he is thought just, and therefore bears rule in the city; he can marry whom he will ... and at every contest ... he gets the better of his antagonists, and gains at their expense, and is rich ... and therefore he is likely to be dearer than they are to the gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the plausible advantages attributed to a successful unjust life (power, wealth, social advantages, religious honors) — these are the stakes in Glaucon's challenge and must be addressed when evaluating justice's worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of conventional praise: reputation and rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and tutors are always telling their sons and their wards that they are to be just; but why? not for the sake of justice, but for the sake of character and reputation; in the hope of obtaining for him who is reputed just some of those offices, marriages, and the like ... More, however, is made of appearances by this class of persons than by the others; for they throw in the good opinion of the gods, and will tell you of a shower of benefits which the heavens ... rain upon the pious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that common moral teaching typically motivates justice by expected human and divine rewards rather than by demonstrating its intrinsic goodness — a methodological warning to exclude reputational rewards when testing justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of poets, prophets, and rites on moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The poets are the authorities to whom they appeal, now smoothing the path of vice with the words of Hesiod ... And mendicant prophets go to rich men’s doors and persuade them that they have a power committed to them by the gods of making an atonement for a man’s own or his ancestor’s sins by sacrifices or charms ... and these have great power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies cultural mechanisms (poetry, prophecy, rituals, mysteries) that shape beliefs about virtue and vice and thereby alter incentives; relevant when assessing whether people pursue justice for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance vs. truth as determinant of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since then, as philosophers prove, appearance tyrannizes over truth and is lord of happiness, to appearance I must devote myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents the criterion that, in ordinary human calculation, reputation/appearance often outweighs truth in producing what people call a happy life — a diagnostic for why injustice coupled with appearance can be preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological principle: examine the State before the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: justice, which is the subject of our enquiry, is, as you know, sometimes spoken of as the virtue of an individual, and sometimes as the virtue of a State. And is not a State larger than an individual? Then in the larger the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily discernible. I propose therefore that we enquire into the nature of justice and injustice, first as they appear in the State, and secondly in the individual, proceeding from the greater to the lesser and comparing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes the investigative strategy: construct and study a 'city' (larger instance) to see justice at scale because its parts and relations make the nature of justice clearer than in solitary individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and structure of the State: division of labour and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: A State, I said, arises, as I conceive, out of the needs of mankind; no one is self‑sufficing, but all of us have many wants ... one man is a husbandman, another a builder, some one else a weaver ... And if so, we must infer that all things are produced more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him and does it at the right time ... Then carpenters, and smiths, and many other artisans, will be sharers in our little State ... there must be another class of citizens who will bring the required supply from another city ... To secure such an exchange ... they will buy and sell ... a money‑token for purposes of exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives economic and institutional criteria for constructing a city: needs create roles (husbandmen, artisans, merchants, sailors, retailers, hirelings), specialization improves quality/quantity, and markets/money mediate exchange — foundational for tracing justice in social relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy vs. luxurious city: scope affects occupations and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: the true and healthy constitution of the State is the one which I have described. But if you wish also to see a State at fever‑heat ... for in such a State we shall be more likely to see how justice and injustice originate ... the arts of the painter and the embroiderer will have to be set in motion, and gold and ivory and all sorts of materials must be procured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes a basic (healthy) city from a luxurious/expanded one and notes that adding luxuries multiplies occupations, expands borders, and changes social dynamics — a criterion for exploring how complexity and desire shape the emergence of injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity as the generator of social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: I propose therefore that we enquire into the nature of justice ..., for to do so, as I am inclined to think, will be a very serious task. ... Then, as we have many wants, and many persons are needed to supply them, one takes a helper for one purpose and another for another; and when these partners and helpers are gathered together in one habitation the body of inhabitants is termed a State ... the true creator is necessity, who is the mother of our invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames an explanatory criterion: social institutions (the State, occupations, markets) arise from human necessities; this causal principle guides the construction used to analyze justice.
